title: The Button Has Betrayed You
description: A guided investigation into how a visible browser failure becomes evidence, a hypothesis, a targeted fix, and a verified result.

objectives.statement: Separate observable browser evidence from assumptions about a failure.
Form a causal debugging hypothesis from a visible symptom and runtime evidence.
Make a targeted code change and verify that the original behavior works.

content.title: Account settings, apparently saved
content.hook: You changed your display name and clicked Save Changes. The button has other plans.
content.context:
ACCOUNT SETTINGS

Display name: Ada
Email: ada@example.com

[ Save Changes ]

The interface looks ordinary. Click the button in the preview and notice exactly what happens before we explain anything.

content.question: You clicked Save Changes. What should happen?

options.text: The settings should save and a confirmation should appear.
The browser should close the page.
The button should change color, but nothing else.
Nothing can happen because buttons are only visual.

feedback.correct: Good prediction. Keep that expectation visible while we compare it with reality.
feedback.incorrect: Start with the user-visible contract: Save Changes should produce a confirmation.

content.title: The browser disagrees with your expectation
content.text: The click is real, but no confirmation appears. The page does not navigate, the name does not change, and the button does not report success. That is the failure we can investigate.

callout.text: Do not call it broken yet. First record what you can observe.

content.question: Which statements are observable evidence after the click? Select all that apply.

feedback.correct: Exactly. These are observations; the cause is still a hypothesis.
feedback.incorrect: Separate what your eyes can establish from what you are inferring.

content.title: The browser keeps a working representation
content.description: The browser turns source into a representation you can inspect. A temporary change to that representation can change what you see without changing the original source.

layers.name: Rendered page
layers.role: Pixels and controls you can interact with

interactive.caption: Inspecting the representation is evidence gathering, not editing the original file.

content.title: HTML becomes DOM, then a rendered page
content.text: The browser reads HTML and builds a DOM representation. It combines that representation with CSS and JavaScript to produce the page you see. Inspecting the DOM shows the browser's current model; it does not prove the source file is correct.
content.keyTakeaway: HTML → DOM → rendered page. The visible symptom is the starting point for a causal investigation.

content.question: Where should you investigate next to explain a click that produced no confirmation?

options.text: Inspect the button and its event behavior.
Change random CSS until the page looks different.
Refresh and hope the bug disappears.
Inspect the Console for runtime evidence.
Guess that the server is broken.

feedback.correct: Evidence first. The element and Console can tell us what actually happened.
feedback.incorrect: Choose an investigation that can produce evidence about the click.

content.title: The Console has a clue
content.prompt: Reproduce the click, then use the runtime evidence to identify the missing cause.
content.bugDescription: The click handler fails before the confirmation can be shown.
hints: Read the first meaningful error, not the symptom.
Look at the function name the browser cannot find.

testCases.description: Runtime evidence identifies the missing saveChanges function

feedback.correct: We found evidence: ReferenceError: saveChanges is not defined.
feedback.incorrect: Use the runtime message to name the missing identifier precisely.

content.prompt: Form a hypothesis: connect the click, the missing saveChanges identifier, and the absent confirmation in one causal explanation.

feedback.correct: That is a causal hypothesis: symptom → mechanism → cause → outcome.
feedback.incorrect: Mention the click, the failed lookup of saveChanges, and why confirmation never appears.

content.title: Make the smallest useful change
content.prompt: Repair the handler so the Save Changes click can call the function that exists.
content.instructions: Change the event binding to call handleSave, then Run and inspect the result.

files.name: settings.js

testCases.description: The listener references the defined handler

feedback.correct: Targeted change made. Run it before calling the fix verified.
feedback.incorrect: Compare the name used by the listener with the function that is actually defined.

content.prompt: What output should this code produce when the button handler runs?

feedback.correct: Now verify the original behavior, not just the code change.
feedback.incorrect: A verified fix should remove the runtime error and produce the expected confirmation.

content.prompt: The button was not actually broken. Explain what caused the visible failure using symptom → mechanism → cause → outcome.

feedback.correct: You explained the mechanism, not just the vocabulary.
feedback.incorrect: Include the click event, the lookup for saveChanges, the ReferenceError, and the missing confirmation.

content.title: Transfer: Invite teammate
content.prompt: A different interface has a broken Invite teammate button. Reproduce the symptom, inspect the evidence, form a hypothesis, and repair the smallest cause.
content.bugDescription: The button appears, but clicking it produces no invitation confirmation.

files.name: invite.js

fixRequirements: Use the runtime evidence to identify the undefined handler
Bind the click to the defined function

testCases.description: Invite button references the defined sendInvite function

feedback.correct: You transferred the workflow: reproduce, observe, hypothesize, fix, verify.
feedback.incorrect: Do not guess. Inspect the handler name, make a targeted repair, and verify the result.

content.title: You learned how to find out
takeaways: Observe the symptom before explaining it.
Form a causal hypothesis from runtime evidence.
Make one targeted change, then verify the original behavior.
nextSteps: Use the same workflow on the next unfamiliar bug.

content.title: Capability demonstrated
content.message: You can investigate a browser failure instead of guessing: observe, gather evidence, form a hypothesis, change one thing, and verify.
nextSteps: Carry this workflow to the next unfamiliar interface.
